#2002. 'We owe it to Michael Carrick': Kobbie Mainoo lays down the gauntlet for his Man United team-mates - and claims they are just ONE win away from transforming their season

Published: 10:37 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 14:14 EDT, 2 November 2026

Kobbie Mainoo says Manchester United’s stars owe it to head coach Michael Carrick and the fans to turn their season around – and believe it might only take one win.

United go into Tuesday’s Champions League tie against Roma at Old Trafford without a victory in nine games and hovering one place above the Premier League relegation zone.

It has left Carrick fighting for his job and led to fans turning on the players after the last home game against Bournemouth which ended with a 3-0 defeat.

Carrick has done his best to shield the squad from criticism, and Mainoo said: ‘I feel like our way to repay that is to also be behind the manager on the pitch and off it, and fight for us as a team.

‘In these tough times you can't expect the fans 100,000 per cent of the time to be happy and cheering when we're not putting out results, you know. We owe it to them to put the results out there for them to cheer again.

‘Of course, it's been a tough season. We've not had the results we've wanted, but you know we need to look forward now. There are big, big games ahead and I feel like we're one win away from changing that.

Kobbie Mainoo says Manchester United’s stars owe it to Michael Carrick and the fans to turn their season around

‘I've been at this club for a long time and I know there's always going to be ups and downs. It's never going to be plain sailing and smooth to the top. So you expect bumps and the best thing about them is you're able to bounce back from them.’

Mainoo signed a new five-year contract in April after re-establishing himself at his boyhood club under Carrick, having asked to leave under the previous head coach Ruben Amorim.

Despite the club’s fortunes taking a nosedive this season, the 21-year-old is determined to help restore the standards that made United great.

‘I'm very grateful to the boss for putting the trust in me as soon as he came in, putting that belief in me and giving me all the advice that he has,’ added Mainoo, who returned to action at Chelsea on Saturday after missing five games.

‘Knowing he's a player who's been at this club and knows the history of this club and knows what it takes to win, I take those words to heart and I try and apply them every day in training and in games.

‘United's a huge club, so I think a lot of people know the values that this club holds and that have been passed down through the people who've worked and played here. I feel like I take some responsibility in that and in spreading the word of what is Manchester United, coming up through the academy. I plan to send that message for hopefully as long as I can.

‘I've tried to take on more responsibility in the team. I want to impose myself more in games and they've definitely helped to do that, giving me more responsibility with taking the ball. There have been ups and downs, but I have to have belief in myself even in these tough times.

‘I feel like in every period of my career so far, I've tried to take positives from them. Even, you know, times that I'm not playing I've learned things and I'm still applying them to this day.’

Fulham endured a winless six-game start in the Premier League this season, but a timely upturn in form for head coach Alvaro Arbeloa has seen his team put together a three-game unbeaten run, while they have lost just one of their last six matches in the top tier (W2 D3).

Arbeloa is encouraged to see his players believing in the way he wants his team to play and hopes that the Cottagers – sitting 15th in the table and only two points above the relegation zone – will begin “a long journey” in the right direction as they bid to steer themselves away from danger.

Although Fulham have scored the joint third-fewest goals in the Premier League this season (nine), they have made notable improvements in defence, conceding just three goals across their last six league games, while no other club has conceded fewer goals than the Cottagers (11) among sides currently sitting in the bottom eight this term.

Fulham will welcome Saturday’s clash with Newcastle, as they have won three of their last four top-flight meetings with the Magpies (L1), having previously gone eight matches without a victory (D2 L6).

Sitting down in 13th spot and just four points above the bottom three, Newcastle will be keen to bounce back with a morale-boosting win against a Fulham side below them in the table, as testing fixtures against Arsenal, Brighton, Man United and rivals Sunderland will follow after the international break.

After beating Crystal Palace 2-0 in their most recent PL away match, the Magpies will endeavour to win back-to-back top-flight games on the road for the first time since April 2025 when they travel to Craven Cottage, while the fact that each of their last four away league wins have come in London bodes well ahead of Saturday’s contest.

Hugo Larsson and Cesar Palacios are both pushing for a start in centre-midfield, but Arbeloa may decide to stick with Shea Charles and Sander Berge in deeper positions with Joshua King operating as a number 10.

Although Gonzalo Garcia has failed to score in his last eight Premier League starts, the former Real Madrid may keep his place as the central striker, forcing Rodrigo Muniz to watch on from the substitutes’ bench once again.

#1998. Project 2035 sounds good but Scottish women’s football needs more than bold promises

A hefty dose of cynicism is always healthy whenever a politician turns up to kick a ball about with a group of kids for the cameras.

John Swinney got to work on his keepie-uppie skills this week at Easter Road as Project 2035 was rolled out in an initiative between the Scottish government and the SFA, among others, with the long-term ambitions of the project comfortably ticking the “ambitious in outlook” box.

It would be hard to find fault with the bold objectives that have been set for the next decade.

There were the immediate headline takeaways; doubling the number of registered female players in the country and quadrupling attendances at matches jumped out. Key, too, is regular qualification for major tournaments – and making an impact when qualification has been secured.

In terms of a manifesto that is exciting and visionary, there was much to be pleased about. But, as ever, the proof will be in the pudding. And when it comes to past behaviours predicting future outcomes, it would have to be said Scotland have excelled at taskforces and not quite so much at outcomes.

The initial outlay from the government is £250,000 for this year. That will cover the first step of their contribution but across the remaining terms until 2035 – by which time Scotland will hope to be co-hosts at the Women’s World Cup – the reality is that if those ambitions are to come to fruition, then pockets will need to be pretty deep.

It will take a lot of work and a lot of joined-up thinking across the board but the key to it all, as ever, is money.

The reality just now is this is a Scotland national team who have not qualified for a major tournament since 2019. There has been a regression in the SWPL both in terms of attendances, media exposure, quality and standard of players.

The league itself is split in terms of those who can afford to offer full-time professional contracts and those who can pay a tenner a week for expenses. A full-time professional SWPL may well be the first major step towards any quest to take the country to a level where it is fulfilling the objectives that were set out this week.

As it stands, that possibility would seem to be light years away.

It is not all doom and gloom. Scotland coach Melissa Andreatta has injected more than just enthusiasm and positivity into the national set-up. Initial impressions of her impact are positive, as witnessed by an unbeaten Nations League campaign and a return to League A.

Brazil next summer is the big one. Getting past Sweden in a two-legged World Cup play-off final next month would be the biggest result in Scotland’s history. It is fair to say it is a monumental challenge that lies ahead.

Caroline Weir has been shortlisted in successive years for the Ballon d’Or while Erin Cuthbert captains Chelsea in the WSL. Kim Little’s time with the national team has long since passed but that trio provide compelling evidence that Scotland have been able to produce world-class players.

But as the game has developed at a rate of knots elsewhere, it has stagnated in Scotland.

Lessons have to be learned from 2019, from the way that 18,555 fans turned up to wave Scotland off to France for their first World Cup to a collapse in interest and exposure within months. To understand how to get it right, there needs to be an understanding of where it went wrong.

The approach from government bodies to work in tandem with the SFA is sensible. The benefits of women retained in sport, not even at elite level but simply a recreational level, have a huge societal knock-on effect.

But it will need more than platitudes in front of cameras. The real work will be done in the nitty-gritty, day-to-day work. And elevating Scotland to the levels spoken about this week ultimately requires significant investment.

Megan Rapinoe has always been Marmite-like; observers either love her frank outspokenness or find their hackles rising on the back of it.

There are some arguments to suggest a woman with strong opinions she isn’t afraid to share will always invite a backlash. In any case, Rapinoe, so central for so long to such a successful USWNT as she claimed two World Cups and an Olympic goal medal, has been consistent that she sees no issue with trans athletes, a conversation that never seems to be too far from the surface in women’s sport.

Rapinoe’s argument centred on the idea there is no fairness in sport, citing the natural advantages of 7-foot-4-inch basketball player Victor Wembanyama as her example.

The problem with that comparison, however, is it fundamentally misses the point that biological males have a distinct advantage when it comes to competing.

Kelly Clark found herself out of Celtic’s starting line-up across recent weeks. The first Celtic women’s captain to lead the club to a title and the first to take them

into the Champions League, one suspects that finding herself on the bench would have been a sobering experience, and novel given the fact

she has been a mainstay of this Celtic team.

Drafted back into the starting XI, she produced a big goal for Grant Scott’s side on Wednesday night as she gave the Parkhead side a win over Hibs at Meadowbank.

Plenty of life in her yet, it would seem.

#1994. John Clark's granddaughter opens up on bid to immortalise Lisbon Lion with statue

"People knew the Lisbon Lion, but to me he was just grandad"’ says Clare Clark, articulating how it felt to be the apple of the eye of a Celtic legend.

“I still tear up every time I think or talk about him. It has been really hard since he left us last year. He was just such a big part of my life.”

John Clark passed away at the age of 84 in June last year. A surgeon in urology, his granddaughter still finds it hard to process the loss.

As a medical student at Aberdeen University, she would maintain the long-established practice of calling the old Bhoy every night at 10pm. Just to check in and get a rundown on his day.

“I actually called him Gan Gan. He was always just Gan Gan to me. So much so that when my mum or my gran talk about him even now they still refer to him as GG. It stuck.

“He was one of the driest and funniest men you could meet. He would always have a sly wee one liner that he delivered so softly it was easy to miss it altogether.”

The best story told about Clark – Luggy to friends and team-mates – dates back to the summer of 1981. Celtic were in New York to compete in the Trans-Atlantic Challenge Cup, a four team pre-season tournament also featuring the New York Cosmos, Seattle Sounders and Southampton.

In a hotel lift, winger Davie Provan was standing with the club’s assistant manager of the time when the doors opened and Pele, arguably the greatest footballer of all time, walked in.

Performing promotion duties for Escape To Victory, the Brazilian icon recognised a former opponent from a friendly international between Scotland and Brazil at Hampden prior to the 1966 World Cup.

“Scotland, Hampden, you number six – a very good player,” said Pele in warm tones. The unassuming Clark shook the great man’s hand in acknowledgement and smiled politely.

When the lift reached his floor, Pele walked away with a final wave. The doors closed and Clark turned to Provan – the winger’s jaw still pinned to the floor – and asked straight-faced, “Who the hell was that?”

A football anorak, he had an encyclopedic memory for dates, opponents and games. Wagging a finger in the air, he would recall the name of a guy he marked in 1964 as if it was yesterday. If he failed to recognise Pele, it was a first.

Marink Reedijk lays down Aberdeen challenge to Hibs team after Hearts win It pushes you forward – Jacob Murrell feeling fuelled by Falkirk fan fervour

Confirming the veracity of the story, his granddaughter tells The Fixture: “My mum always told me that lift story was true. He used to laugh about it.” Most people did, to be fair.

For the best part of six decades, Clark served Celtic as a player, coach, assistant manager, long-standing kit man and club ambassador. Willie Maley might be the only man in Celtic’s history to give more years of his life to the club.

A central defender who formed a formidable partnership with Billy McNeill, he was just five foot eight and referred to almost everyone he met as “big man”. Yet, when he passed away, it felt like the Scottish game had lost a gentle giant.

A winner of four league titles, four League Cups and three Scottish Cups, his crowning glory was Lisbon 1967 when Celtic were crowned champions of Europe.

The 60th anniversary of that Inter Milan victory falls next May, with Jim Craig, Bobby Lennox and Willie Wallace the only Lions still alive to mark the occasion. Craig spoke in these pages of his own battle with Alzheimer’s this year and all three

Lions face health challenges likely to limit their involvement in the celebrations.

For the Clark family, last year’s loss will only add to the poignancy and, in a quest to preserve his memory, the John Clark Legacy Trust has been established to raise funds for a statue in his honour.

A special charity walk is scheduled for three stages on Saturday, November 21. The first stage will cover Chapelhall to Billy McNeill’s statue in Bellshill. The second will move to Jimmy Johnstone’s plinth in Viewpark. The final leg will see those taking part walk to Celtic Park.

“Grandad would have said, ‘I don’t want people to put themselves out’.

“He would say, ‘You don’t need to do that’.

“He would have thought there were more remarkable people who deserved it more than him…”

Celtic supporters would disagree with that sentiment. Signing for the club at the age of 17, Clark’s first appearance came at Arbroath’s Gayfield in 1959 and his first goal in a Scottish Cup replay at Hibernian two years later. Between April of 1965 and September ’67 he turned out in 140 consecutive matches with no injuries, no squad rotation. If he was fit, he played.

Where other members of Jock Stein’s greatest team were natural extroverts who revelled in wine, women and song, Clark was more considered; an unassuming man with a dry sense of humour who was uncomfortable in the spotlight.

“He was always a very hands-on grandad,” adds Clare. “He went under the radar. He wouldn’t do anything to be big or flashy.

“I remember the day he unfurled the league flag at Parkhead [in 2015] and he was nervous because he didn’t know how people would react to him doing it. He was humble like that.”

A Parkhead regular from the age of three, a matchday ticket would usually come with a £10 or £20 note attached without fuss or ceremony.

“It was always just the small gestures he preferred. We high fived on Christmas Day because we were never a touchy-feely family. But that was how he was, undemonstrative.

“He was quietly there in the background if you needed anything and he was one of the kindest and most patient people. So much so that I probably had him wrapped around my finger at times.”

Clark’s own father, John senior, was a railway engineer who died in an accident in Watford when his son was just 10.

Thrust into the role of bread-winner for his mother and siblings, a local farmer allowed him to sell eggs and potatoes to make ends meet.

“During the 50th anniversary celebrations for the Lisbon Lions, the BBC did a documentary and that was the first time we as a family had really heard my grandad talk about the loss of his father,” said Clare.

“It had probably affected him more than he wanted to say. But I don’t know if he would have been the man he was without going through those hardships.

“His siblings Michael, Maureen and Margaret are still here and they idolised him because he had to stand up and do things he didn’t want to do.

“Aunt Margaret has no memory of her dad. And granddad kind of filled that role for her. He always wanted to do the best for his family.”

John Clark in action for Celtic (Image: Colorsport / Shutterstock)

Clark actually had two families in life. The first was his wife Eileen, children Martin and Marie and their three grandchildren. The other were the band of brothers famously assembled from within a 30-mile radius of Glasgow to become the first British winners of the European Cup.

There are times, now, when the current team’s performances and results in UEFA club competitions feel like an affront to the memory of the halcyon days. While Thursday’s win over Besiktas avoided a record run of five straight defeats in Europe, the 60th anniversary will serve as a stark reminder of how far standards have fallen.

“It will be hard next year for a number of reasons,” says Clare. “It probably will be the last big anniversary with any of the Lions there.

“They are getting older and there is a personal side to that. We are really close with the family of Bobby Lennox, one of the last living lions.

“When grandad was alive, he would speak to Bobby every day. During Covid they would be on the phone a couple of times a day, it was the thing that kept them going.

“You would hear grandad telling Bobby to make sure he got out and got his steps in round the garden or discussing a game on the TV.

“They were like brothers actually. And we know the McNeill family well, because we were all in Aberdeen together. And it’s sad there are not many Lions left now.

“This 60th anniversary will be very different from the 50th, that’s for sure.”

Approached by North Lanarkshire Council last year, the John Clark Legacy Trust is not the first established to raise money for a Lisbon Lions statue. It is the most recent.

Jim Goodwin says Dundee Utd are eager to keep momentum going against Motherwell Celtic's 'Che Guevaras' should show their fellow fans some respect at this year's AGM

“We want to get the statue in Chapelhall, the same way as Billy [McNeill] has one in Bellshill, Bobby [Lennox] has one in Saltcoats and Tommy [Gemmell] has one in Craigneuk,” said Clare.

The estimated cost of the memorial will be £120,000, with council grants and a series of fundraising events assisting the cause. Roughly 21 kilometres, the charity walk is expected to take five hours and any additional money raised will be put to use in the Chapelhall community.

“We want to carry on pursuing the issues that grandad valued and he really did value the people of Chapelhall,” added Clare.

“Everyone knew him even though he hadn’t lived there for 40 years.

“In this day and age, with the cost of living and putting children through football training every week, kids who are not going to be the next Celtic or Rangers stars still deserve the opportunity to play the game.

“Our plan is to work with local schools and teams to help fund their programmes to get as many young players as possible involved in the game. I think that’s what granddad would have wanted.”

For details of how to donate to the John Clark Legacy Trust email: johnclarklegacytrust@gmail.com

#1993. Stephen Robinson proud of his battling Dons but injury crisis deepens

Published: 17:30 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 14:43 EDT, 2 November 2026

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson has revealed his injury crisis has become even more catastrophic ahead of the weekend league visit of Hibernian that has the potential to make or break his reign.

The Dons manager saw his side put in a fine, disciplined display in going down 1-0 to Rangers in the Premier Sports Cup final, but lost Emmanuel Gyamfi within 15 minutes after he collided with Kim Min-su and also has Brad Lyons battling a knock.

Robinson admitted afterwards that there is no chance of longer-term absentees Chris Cadden, Mats Knoester and Lewis Mayo being available, with Dan Happe the only player likely to return for the Saturday night showdown with Premiership bottom dogs Hibs after being suspended last night.

‘Gyamfi will be out for a long period of time,’ reported Robinson. ‘It looked like it was maybe the other thigh that he’s had a problem with. It’s a heartbreaker for the boy.

‘Brad Lyons took a really bad knock. I’m not sure how serious that is. Hopefully, he’s got away with it.

‘Chris Cadden will be out for six weeks. Mats Knoester is four to six weeks.

Emmanuel Gyamfi limped off early with an injury in Aberdeen's semi-final defeat

‘The only plus point is Dan Happe. It’s very difficult because half the squad are not available. Any team that does well, there’s consistency and patience.

‘Over time, the last person that had prolonged success in Aberdeen was Derek (McInnes). He was given a lot of time and a lot of support, but we’ve not been able to put a consistent team, never mind a consistent shape, on the pitch.

‘It’s four changes every week at the moment.’

Robinson, however, stated his pride in the way his players performed and backed centre-back Jack Milne while taking a pop at the criticism he has come in for of late.

‘They rose against adversity this time. They put in a real performance,’ he said.

‘Rangers scored during our best spell in the game, which is unfortunate, but it’s been a tough week for us with injuries, really tough.

‘They showed great character and courage.

‘Jack’s a young man. Surprisingly, he’s from Aberdeen and he still gets an incredible amount of stick.

‘He’s had one full season and he’s a lovely boy that wants to learn. He’s just learning the game. I thought he showed real character.’

Dons boss Stephen Robinson on the touchline in the 1-0 defeat to Rangers

Robinson also refused to criticise captain Kevin Nisbet after seeing him pass up a couple of golden chances.

‘If you want chances to fall to anyone, it’s Kevin and he had the opportunity to play Mitchy Ntelo in with one of them when clean through,’ he reflected.

‘We had grown into the game. We were organised defensively despite not knowing what our team would be until Saturday morning.

‘I’m proud of the players because they gave me absolutely everything.

‘You’d need to ask the fans if they saw positive performances. I can only answer for myself. I saw a group of boys give everything in adversity.

‘Everyone expected us to roll over and get battered but that wasn’t the case. They’ve shown they have the character to play for Aberdeen in big games, no doubt.’

#1992. Wrexham vs Wolverhampton Wanderers - prediction, team news, lineups

By Oliver Thomas | 05 Nov 2026 21:00, Last updated: 07 Nov 2026 11:09

Two Championship teams seeking to build on midweek victories lock horns at the Racecourse Ground on Saturday lunchtime as Wrexham play host to Wolverhampton Wanderers.

April 1988 was the last time these two sides faced off down in the fourth tier of English football, with the Dragons securing a 4-2 home win over the Old Gold.

After suffering back-to-back Championship defeats without scoring against Blackburn Rovers (2-0) and Sheffield United (1-0), Wrexham produced a significantly improved performance to earn a surprise 2-0 home triumph over league leaders Middlesbrough on Wednesday night.

Second-half strikes from George Thomason and substitute Oliver Rathbone inspired the Dragons to “upset a good team” in the words of manager – and boyhood Boro fan – Phil Parkinson, who dedicated the result to his ill father back home in Stockton-on-Tees.

Wrexham’s timely and morale-boosting victory has once again demonstrated that Parkinson is at his best when the pressure is at its highest following an inconsistent run of results this term (W4 D5 L5).

Three of Wrexham’s four Championship wins after 14 games this season have come at home, and they now sit 16th in the table, seven points clear of the relegation zone and eight points adrift of the playoffs.

Another tricky test against high-flying Wolves is up next for Wrexham on Saturday, but the hosts will back themselves to make the net ripple at the Racecourse Ground where they have proved to be a prolific unit in front of their own fans, scoring in 17 of their 18 competitive home fixtures this calendar year – a 2-0 loss to Millwall in February represents the only blot on their copybook.

Wolves continue to enhance their status as one of the promotion favourites in the Championship this season, after securing a hard-fought 2-1 comeback victory over Bristol City at Ashton Gate on Tuesday night.

Trailing with just eight minutes of normal time remaining, Newcastle loanee Sean Neave came off the bench to score his first two senior goals, including an 89th-minute winner, to turn the contest on its head in dramatic fashion.

Cesar Peixoto’s side have climbed to second in the table, and victory over Wrexham this weekend would see them momentarily leapfrog Middlesbrough to the second-tier summit before the current leaders face Watford a few hours later on Saturday.

Wolves travel to the North East of Wales in formidable form, winning six and drawing one of their last eight Championship outings (L1), while they have also found the back of the net in 13 of their 14 league matches this term, scoring at least twice in eight of those.

The Old Gold currently boast the joint-best away record in the Championship having accumulated 13 points from seven games on the road – level with four other clubs – and they are now aiming to win their first-ever away match against Wrexham at the fourth time of asking (D2 L1).

Wolverhampton Wanderers Championship form:

Wolverhampton Wanderers form (all competitions):

Wrexham striker Sam Smith is facing a "significant" spell in the sidelined with a knee injury, so Kieffer Moore is expected to continue as the central striker, with Bailey Cadamarteri providing cover.

Forwards Josh Windass (ankle) and Nathan Broadhead (thigh) both remain out injured, while midfielder Callum O'Hare (fitness) will be assessed ahead of kickoff after missing the last two games.

Dominic Hyam and Zak Vyner could be recalled at the expense of Joe Worrall and Max Cleworth at centre-back, and Matty James will battle with George Dobson for a start in midfield, while Rathbone will hope to force his way back into the final third after scoring as a substitute in midweek.

As for Wolves, Peixoto is hopeful that midfielder Jordan James will be available after the international break as a hamstring injury forced the Welshman to miss the win at Bristol City.

With Raul Jimenez still out with a long-term ankle injury, Adam Armstrong could be handed his fourth successive start up front, but he now faces stern competition from Neave following his late brace in midweek.

Mateus Mane will hope to replace Rafiki Said on the left side of attack, while Nasser Djiga will likely battle with Yerson Mosquera for a start at centre-back alongside Ladislav Krejci.

Patterson; Vyner, Hyam, Doyle; Kabore, James, Whiteman, Ekomie; O'Hare, Rathbone; Moore

Wolverhampton Wanderers possible starting lineup:

Sa; Trippier, Djiga, Krejci, Bueno; Andre, Munetsi; Bellegarde, Lopez, Mane; Armstrong

Wrexham and Wolves enter this intriguing contest in high spirits and have proven throughout this season that they boast a consistent goal threat, so we expect the net to ripple at both ends of the pitch this weekend.

However, the Old Gold will be regarded as favourites and we expect Peixoto's men to build on their strong run of form by claiming all three points from their visit to Wales.

#1991. From Hibs casual to a sold-out Hydro - the incredible story of bare-knuckle boxing's Leith Warrior

The hands might tell a story although Lewis Knox will hope they know when to stop blabbing. After all, he doesn't want his tools of the trade to betray him.

These fists helped him survive on Leith’s mean streets. As a former Hibs casual, he once used them to defend his club’s honour.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In a more legitimate context, one less likely to interest the authorities, they are crucial for his current job installing sofas up and down the country. And more pressingly, in Glasgow on Saturday, these hands will be used as weapons with the aim of drawing blood.

“All legal and above board,” Knox clarifies. Welcome to the world of “BKFC”, which stands for Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship. The promotion, co-owned by controversial UFC star Conor McGregor, hits Scotland for the first time this weekend.

Only the All Blacks’ visit to Murrayfield, Celtic v Kilmarnock and possibly Aberdeen v Hibs will attract a bigger crowd in a sporting context.

Still, it’s guaranteed none of those involved in these fixtures will have spent the start of this week lugging sofas up and down stairwells. “I install them into houses from Berwick-Upon-Tweed to near enough Stonehaven," says Knox. "12-hour shifts, 7 am to 7 pm. Four days on, four days off. But I am still training every night. As well as being a dad of three."

Even the All Blacks, who have been utilising the gym where Knox has been training under the watchful eye of Ali Thomson, might wince at the thought of this schedule. Thomson describes Knox as a "phenomenon". He complains his own arms are aching from doing pads with the focused fighter in the run-up to this weekend.

"People say things are impossible,” ponders Knox. “But you know if you really want it? Things can be done. My mum, my dad, my family. They all support me. Everyone is tuned into it. They all try to help out. This is not an overnight thing, this has been three years in the making to get to where I am now. I have worked so hard."

He was in Fife as recently as Monday delivering sofas but who knows where he will be this time next year? The bare-knuckle scene is taking off, boosted by McGregor's involvement. "I'd like to turn pro," says Knox, 29. Remember that Hearts fan ridiculed for claiming on camera that he’d be willing to have his hands chopped off if it meant his team winning the league?

Knox loves Hibs. He was thrilled by last weekend’s League Cup semi-final win over Hearts at Hampden, which he watched on TV because he was deep in fight camp. However, he can’t afford to strike any bargain involving the prospect of losing his hands. As a bare-knuckle boxer on the cusp of his biggest ever fight, they are, after his three children, among the most precious things on earth to him.

Perhaps a little Atrixo might be in order. They are battered, bruised and a little disfigured. Hardly surprising really, since they are used to pound his opponents. “Bone on bone,” he says. “There is nothing more raw.” He reports that he hasn't broken his hands in his last three fights. "They are solid, like sledgehammers," he says.

Rather than slathering them with hand cream, Knox is considering the old fighters’ trick of sticking his hands into a bucket of sand – or rice. “It strengthens up the skin,” he says.

He broke two knuckles in his very first (official) bare-knuckle fight three years ago this month. Slightly horrifyingly, these knuckles now appear to have disappeared completely. “Yeah, disintegrated,” he says. “Two knuckles have gone, one has dipped (into the hand). As for my pinkie, I can’t stretch it out."

Knox demonstrates this inability to extend his little finger in the café where we are sitting. The Leith Warrior, as he’s known, has ordered a flat white with a shot of caramel (there was still plenty of time to make the required fighting weight of 66 kgs). If not for the damage to his hands, he seems incredibly unwarrior-like.

Softly spoken and trim, almost delicate-looking, the tattoos extending past his collar line on his neck are perhaps the main evidence of a life lived on the edge.

“I always wanted tattoos,” he says. As one suspects is the case with many people, he first succumbed to the needle and ink on holiday in Magaluf.

“A star on my chest and a Hibs tattoo on the back of my calf,” he says. “I thought I had to get serious ones after that. Ones devoted to my gran and my grandad, who both played huge parts in my life from a young age. I also have a gladiator on my arm and neck tattoos…It has become part of the job!”

As for the colours he sports when competing in the circular four-rope ring, which is designed to encourage fast-paced bouts, it wasn’t up for discussion. “Green and white, I always represent where I am from,” he says. “And a Hibs badge on my shorts. I am never not representing Leith.

“I grew up in Leith, a lot of gang culture, an environment of violence as a young boy,” he continues. “You had to be streetwise from a young age I suppose. Leith has its good and bad sides. For me, it’s one of the best places in the world. But it can be one of the worst places in the world.

"Knife crime, drugs. It’s a mix of cultures, backgrounds. I grew up in all of that. But I was never ultra-violent.”

His mother, Niki, once ran the Junction bar. Knox enjoys an obvious status in the area. A taxi driver beeps his horn as soon as he steps out of the door of our meeting place on Easter Road. Cross Knoxy and you cross Leith.

He knows people, Irvine Welsh included. The author – a more than decent boxer himself - has been mentoring Knox before his featherweight division fight against Tommy “Chaos” Carus from Liverpool at the OVO Hydro on Saturday night. Welsh has already featured in an Instagram video promoting Knox’s fight, playing the role of his manager.

“Oi, Knoxy!” he calls out after taking a phone call. “Get your dancing shoes on! We’ve got ourselves a pagger.”

Knox v Carus, or the Leith Warrior v Chaos, or indeed Scotland v England, is the third fight of 11 on a bill topped by Sean Weir’s light heavyweight title bout with Leigh Cohoon, a late stand-in for Irishman Conor ‘Da Crook’ Cooke.

Cooke’s team cited concerns about the venue layout and ticketing arrangements for their withdrawal. Some have interpreted this as another way of saying they were worried sectarian/football-related hooliganism – Weir was once a member of the Rangers Riot Crew casuals group - could flare.

Almost 11,000 are expected to converge on the Hydro for the event. BKFC is dedicated to “fighter safety”. According to their official bumph, the organisation prides itself in being “the truest form of bare-knuckle fighting”. Fighters are not allowed to wrap their hands to within one inch of the knuckle. This weekend’s spectacle is the first legally sanctioned and regulated bare knuckle event in Scotland.

For the uninitiated, the fights last for five two-minute rounds. If there isn’t a knockout, it tends to be fairly obvious who’s won.

“Cuts,” says Knox. “It comes down to facial damage. Because in boxing or any gloved fight, you can punch them ten times with a glove and not make a mark, you can punch them once with a bare knuckle and split someone’s head open.

“It is about getting as much of that in in a short period of time. The first punch usually sets the tone for the fight. It depends on where you catch him, I suppose. It is all about just getting in there and being horrible.”

It’s easy to question the ethics of unpadded pugilism. However, defenders of this ancient and previously underground practice insist it’s a safer, more honest form of boxing. "It is better for the brain, much better," claims Knox. "In boxing you get the double shock with the glove – boom, boom. It rattles the brain. You don’t see the damage facially necessarily. With bare knuckle, bone is hitting bone. That’s it. The facial damage will be shown. Internally your brain is not getting rattled for 12 rounds.

“It is five rounds of two minutes. If you last that, although you might get a few cuts, your brain is fine. To me, my brain feels fine! In my 50s and 60s I will still have a functional brain. I might have a few scars and a few missing teeth but I move pretty well (to avoid the punches). My nose is still straight...”

Inside the ring might be a veritable haven as the evening hots up on Saturday. “It is like any combat sport,” says Knox. “The crowd can be unpredictable. A bit like a football crowd. I just hope that because this event is so big for Scotland and so big for the bare-knuckle scene and for lads like myself that nothing serious kicks off. There will be some ‘characters’ there, you always get the odd person. You get that anywhere.”

Knox anticipates an unholy commotion when the first bars of Born Slippy strike up. The Underworld track is his walk on song, unsurprisingly given the Trainspotting connotations. Sunshine on Leith just wouldn’t do it in this context. Fine for after last weekend’s win for Hibs at Hampden against Hearts, but perhaps a little too plaintive, a little too pretty, for a night of good-to-honest testosterone-fuelled violence.

As much as the Easter Road club might wish otherwise, a line – if admittedly indirect - can be drawn between Hibs and Knox’s prowess in the ring.

“Before I got into bare knuckle, I boxed," he says. "But I was also fighting in football as well. I grew up in a place where there was a lot of gang culture, an environment of violence as a young boy. You had to be streetwise from a young age I suppose.”

He ran with the Capital City Service – Hibs casuals – from 17-years-old onwards. “I found it attractive,” he says. “It was something I felt I was missing: being part of a brotherhood, a group.”

The casuals scene, including rival groups such as ASC (Aberdeen Soccer Casuals) and Dundee Utility, seems to belong to another era of Scottish football. But the fights still happen, just further away from stadiums.

“Anywhere there isn’t cameras,” he says. “Back in the 80s and most of the 90s, you had groups of a hundred plus. Since TV took over, groups became smaller, more confined, more secret. You had to move with the times I suppose. You couldn’t wander around in groups of hundreds, you’d be seen by all the cameras.”

It became violence by appointment. “You’d phone and say: ‘Meet you there’. A set meet. Sometimes nothing would ever happen. You’d phone all day and nothing would happen. But you’d still have that day out with your mates.”

The arrangements could be painstaking. “It was all planned out. You needed management skills! A lot went into it. You didn’t just turn up and fight. What time were we fighting, what time were the trains, what pubs to go to? It was a lot of work. I could probably pass a management course now quite easily!”

Unlike some, Knox would always endeavour to go the game. He was and remains a football fan and played at a decent level. His first ambition was to be a professional footballer. He played for Hawick Royal Albert and Coldstream in the East of Scotland league – on the wing, wing-back or full-back and then, latterly, as a sweeper with a reputation for never shirking a tackle.

“I was still involved in the casuals scene, still attracted to it,” he says. “It was not all about violence. It was about being with your mates. We dressed the same, liked the same music. Away days having a laugh. It wasn’t all about fighting.”

But some of it undoubtedly was. He remembers once playing in a Scottish Junior Cup tie for Newcraighall, which had kicked off early. “I then went home and got changed before a fight with Raith Rovers, who were playing a Scottish Cup tie against Hibs,” he says.

“Everyone has got a bit older now. The scene has changed. Six guys v six guys, in a forest somewhere. Last team standing wins. To me that’s not football casuals, because you are away from everything.”

“I am not saying football violence is good,” he says. “But there’s so much more to it. It’s guys looking forward to being with their mates, they maybe need that at the end of the week. It’s a release. It acts as therapy for some people.”

The message is: don’t diss what you’ve never tried. The same could apply to bare-knuckle boxing, which is now edging into the mainstream to the extent that this weekend’s extravaganza has been advertised on the side of buses.

Maybe an invite onto the pitch at Hibs before a game might be forthcoming for Knox – it ought to be if he prevails this weekend, which would mean he is the No. 1 contender for the UK featherweight bare-knuckle title.

His ultimate dream is one likely to give Edinburgh city fathers pause. “My goal, my dream fight, if it wasn't Easter Road, would be on the castle esplanade,” he says. “Outdoors, in the summer. It would have a gladiatorial feel about it, you know? That would just be amazing.”

#1990. Newcastle scrape past Millwall to extend Jaissle’s unbeaten start

Joe Willock’s deft finish ensured Newcastle United survived a tough test against Millwall to keep their excellent run in the Carabao Cup intact.

This competition had been fruitful for Newcastle under former manager Eddie Howe and although this match was hard work – as well as hard to watch at times – his successor Matthias Jaissle guided them through a difficult trip to south-east London.

He called it “job done,” and that was pretty much all it was. “We needed patience on one hand, but also to be passionate and tough. We had the chance [to score] and took it,” he said.

Newcastle have reached the semi-finals of this competition three times in the last four years, but struggled to get any sort of tempo going against their Championship opponents.

You could argue the winning goal came against the run of play late in the second half, moments after Millwall substitute Taïryk Arconte had smashed a low shot against the post.

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

Given they were missing 13 players because of injury, this was a brave display from Alex Neil’s side. They frustrated Newcastle for more than an hour, nullifying their attack, to the point where Jaissle’s team looked as though they had run out of ideas.

That was until Lewis Hall combined with Matias Fernandez-Pardo down the left and his drilled cross found Willock who cleverly used the angle to pass the ball into the net. Willock has been rejuvenated under Jaissle. He looked certain to be sold this summer but is now starting regularly under a new manager in the number 10 role his system demands. It has been a nice redemption arc for the former Arsenal academy graduate.

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The victory is all that matters and extends Jaissle’s unbeaten start to five games. Given he arrived just three weeks before the start of the season, that deserves praise even if it is obvious there is a lot of work to be done to improve their offensive play.

Playing in their lilac, or should that be Parma-violet, third kit for the first time, Newcastle looked off colour in the first half. Even though Jaissle named a strong team packed with experience of English cup ties, they struggled to overpower Millwall.

There were a few half-chances as Willock forced a save and Jacob Murphy fired over. There was a header missed from a corner by Sven Botman, which should have hit the target and Yoane Wissa also mistimed his jump after finding space for another header.

Millwall’s two centre-backs, Jake Cooper and Caleb Taylor were immense, flinging themselves in the way of every shot and clearing every loose ball that came into their vicinity. Given their injuries, this was a performance full of fight and defiance from the home side.

However, there was also an absence of quality in the final third from Newcastle, the same lack of cohesion and incision that was apparent at home to Bournemouth last weekend and in the first half away at Tottenham Hotspur.

It meant Millwall were happy to play for set-pieces close to the Newcastle box and Taylor got in front of his marker, flashing a header wide of the post.

That lacklustre first half meant Jaissle’s side had mustered just five shots on target in five halves of football since the 3-2 win over West Bromwich Albion in the previous round of the Carabao Cup.

Millwall started the second period like a side sensing Newcastle were vulnerable. A thunderbolt from Jenson Metcalfe, after the visitors had struggled to clear two crosses, almost gave them a spectacular lead.

Newcastle saw lots of the ball. Millwall were happy enough to let them have it given how little they were hurting them.

So much of Newcastle’s play was slow and cumbersome. Their set-piece delivery was also largely inept.

Neil’s side retained a threat and came so close to taking the lead when, not for the first time, a long ball forward caught the Newcastle defence out of shape and Tino Livramento’s mistake allowed Arconte to run clear and hit the post from a tight angle.

Well in, @Joewillock! 💪 pic.twitter.com/5a8G7lzD3H

Speaking after the game, Millwall manager Alex Neil said: “I’m very proud, I don’t think we deserved to lose that game.

“We had some good moments, and we got done by a bit of sucker punch at the end. But I’m very proud of the lads.”

As for their injury problems, he added: “I didn’t bring the teenagers on as a token gesture, I need to keep the first-team players fit. We’re really at bare bones.

But we beat Bolton at the weekend, got a couple of defeats before that but we started the season really well and once we get everybody back, we’ll be in good shape.”

With the first of the 16 teams through tonight, the draw won’t take place until most of the teams have played next week.

The draw will be shown on Sky Sports on Wednesday 16th Sept, after Manchester United play Brighton. Man City vs Norwich will be the only game outstanding then.

The third round had to be spread over two weeks as the nine Premier League sides in UEFA competitions entered the tournament in this round, as the same time as their Champions League and Europa League fixtures began. To avoid clubs facing clashes, the EFL split the fixtures across the two gameweeks.

Still got some more post-match to come for you, but we’ve got scores from all our matches tonight now:

From the Champions League, Man City held out against Porto to win 2-0.

“I think we had a lot of chances in the first half, and we went in a half-time saying we need to  take our chances, so I’m glad we came out in the second half and we did,” said Willock after the match.

“100% [the competition is important], we’ve won it before so it’s very important to us, but every game is important to us. Especially with a new coach and a lot of new players, we wanted to start the new season well. I think we started really well and we need to continue and this was a big game in keeping that momentum.”

"We said at half-time we NEED to take our chances"Lewis Hall and Joe Willock react to Newcastle's win over Millwall 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/NDF3laD8nT

Take a look at the match-winner from Joe Willock:

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The goal came minutes after Millwall were inches away from taking the lead themselves, as Arconte was denied by the post:

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

We’ll be bringing you more from the post-match now.

Joe Willock has done enough for Newcastle to reach the fourth round and keep the travelling fans singing all the way back to the North-East.

It won’t go down in history as the greatest Carabao fixture, but Newcastle found a way to keep their momentum going and give Matthias Jaissle a win on his cup debut.

Newcastle aren’t taking any risks as Hornicek sends the ball long, and the players keep looking to send the ball down-field.

Seconds to go now. Marschall sends it long for one last effort, but it is cleared out of the box...

Willock has come off now for Newcastle’s own teenager, Sean Steur. A few more minutes and the man now on the bench with have done enough to send his side through to the next round.

We’re into the final minutes as Millwall are throwing everything at this.

Millwall are not out of this yet, as Neghli comes down the left side, twisting his way into the box past his defender – but having done the hard work, his shot flashes low across goal.

Some more changes, as Ramsey comes off for Newcastle, replaced by Lewis Miley.

A double change for the hosts as Dykes and Kelly come off for Regan Monty and Alfie Massey – the former just 15 years old.

Seconds later, another teenager takes to the pitch for Millwall as Osei-Tutu is replaced by 17-year-old Tristan Parkes.

Newcastle almost have another! From the sublime to the ridiculous, as Willock makes another run, this time down the left, and passes the ball onto the edge of the box where Elanga meets it in space. He lets it run, before taking his shot, but it is straight to Marschall.

Finally Newcastle have their breakthrough! They punish Millwall as Fernandez-Pardo feeds Hall on the left, who cuts inside and slips the ball across goal, finding Willock to redirect the ball to slot it home.

Marschall releases Arconte with a long ball and he turns Livramento to find huge amounts of space on the right side. He races into the box and takes a shot from close range, aiming for his near post, but is denied by the woodwork and the rebound hits the seated Hornicek. The keeper is lucky to not concede an own goal, as the ball bounces up and over his leg.

Issoufou again racing down the right side, before cutting inside and taking a shot with his left foot. Hall, who has been so crucial in the Newcastle attack, throws himself at the shot, and it flies high for Hornicek to collect.

Replays show that González, who Millwall players claimed had handled the ball earlier, leant down to clear with his shoulder.

Issoufou sends a great ball in for Millwall from the right side, but it is cleared by a Newcastle player, accompanied by cries for handball.

The game is opening up now as Newcastle make a run of their own, with Willock creating an opening for Elanga to take the ball to the edge of the box, before Taylor slides in to block his shot.

Millwall could absolutely win this with a smash-and-grab with less than 20 minutes to go. They are pushing for it but are lacking some attacking quality to finish the job.

From six shots they’ve had two on target, compared to Newcastle’s three on target from 20.

Fernandez-Pardo gets his first look at the ball, making a very quick run down across the centre of the field to the left side, but Osei-Tutu stays with him and takes him all the way to the back line before giving up a corner.

Elanga takes the corner, punched away by the keeper but no one goes to finish the job and Newcastle get another corner.

Metcalfe, who had his red card overturned this week, is the first player to go in the book for a mistimed challenge on Ramsey.

Just a reminder that there is no extra time, so if we’re all square after 90 minutes, it’s straight to a penalty shoot-out.

Willock gets the ball on the edge of the area and passes it on a quick turn to Barnes just inside the box, but there was not much on his shot and Marschall collects easily.

Double change now for Newcastle as Wissa and Murphy come off, replaced by Elanga and Fernandez-Pardo as Jaissle looks for pace. Schar is handed the armband.

Free kick for Newcastle, right on the corner of the box. Murphy takes, but it hits the wall 10 feet away, and bounces straight back to him. His cross into the box is headed out, and for all the opportunities Newcastle have created, they are yet to find the breakthrough.

We’ve also had a double change for Millwall as Esse and Lovelace have come off, replaced by Issoufou and Arconte.

What colour would you describe this Newcastle away shirt? They look like the sweets Purple Violet to me. Although would you call it an all Lilac number?

It’s the first time they have worn their third kit. Not sure whether I like it or not.  Shame The Den isn’t a sell out although I’m told tickets were priced at £31 and Millwall have a lot of injuries too.

Newcastle get another corner after a run from Willock. The delivery from Hall creates a good amount of confusion in the box and Marschall isn’t sure whether to stay on his line or come out to punch it away. From within the bodies, Wissa tries to get a shot off from close range but it bounces and the keeper easily collects.

González commits another foul, pulling down Esse, to give Millwall another free kick from 40 yards out.

The ball meets Taylor at the back post, but he meets it in the air and can’t quite direct it either into goal or back into the six-yard box, so it goes out for a Newcastle goal kick.

Another half chance for Millwall as Dykes feeds Kelly on the right side, who runs into the box and gets caught between passing the ball in and taking the shot, with the ball going high over the box.

Another great challenge from Osei-Tutu as Willock makes a run into the box, but is brought down by a well-timed tackle from the right-back.

The corner from Hall is better, but headed out and cleared.

Barnes again with space on the left side and he sends a ball fizzing low across the box to the far post but Neghli is able to lean on Murphy to stop him making contact.

Scramble for Newcastle as the ball is sent by Dykes to Neghli free at the far post, who puts the ball into a very dangerous area just in front of goal and everyone jumps on. Newcastle get to it first, managing to clear it from the goal mouth. It is cleared outside the box and it bounces to unmarked Metcalfe, who takes a thunderous shot, putting his laces through the ball but he is unable to keep it down and it goes over the bar.

Despite Alex Neil’s premonitions, no changes for Millwall at the break.

Right-back change for Newcastle, as Dedic comes off and Tino Livramento comes on.

The earlier kick-offs of the Carabao third round have just started their second periods, but here are the latest scores:

Aston Villa won their opening Champions League fixture 3-2 against Club Brugge, while Man City are still goalless against Porto, which you can follow with our live blog here

And that’s the last action of the half, as just one minute was added on and that was taken up by Newcastle’s corner.

Nothing separates the two sides at the half, thought the visitors have dominated in terms of possession and chances.

Millwall have held fast and will be happy to be finishing the half level. We may see some changes from them after the break.

The game is opening up before half-time, and Newcastle go again with Hall and Barnes. Osei-Tutu does well to wait before going in to block Barnes’s shot and send the ball behind for another Newcastle corner.

The delivery is once again poor, but Schar is pulled down inside the box by Taylor and is furious that nothing was given. There’s no VAR so there’s no review to consider – but looking at replays, Millwall were very lucky to get away with that foul.

Cooper makes a perfect pass down the left sideline, allowing Neghli to find space and forcing Newcastle to clear it away fo a Millwall corner.

The ball in is promising but Hornicek gets to it and punches it away, but the hosts keep the pressure on.

Baggott floats another ball across the box towards the right back post, but Hornicek easily collects the ball as Neghli can’t quite connect.

Newcastle moving the ball well again across midfield and it comes to Schar, who runs into space and gets a low shot away, around 40 yards out. It  takes a slight deflection on its way, going just wide of the post.

González is not having his best night and makes a silly foul against Dykes on the sideline, giving the hosts another set piece. The swinging ball in is not nearly as good as last time, and only reaches the first man, Newcastle’s Ramsey.

Millwall get a free kick, and the delivery is good, allowing Taylor to connect on the header inside the box. He beats Hornicek but the header rolls just wide of the post, to the groans of the home fans.

Hall goes short with the corner and Dedic has lots of time to cross the ball in from the right. It’s headed away but Millwall can’t break on the counter.

That sums up the game pretty well: not much finishing quality from Newcastle but Millwall not creating much from their limited spells of possession.

Newcastle pushing again. Another ball pulled back by Barnes finds Ramsey at the top of the box, and his ball in connects with Wissa. Newcastle’s captain can’t head it in the right direction though and Millwall survive again.

The spell of pressure results in another corner for the visitors – and now we’re getting some pushing in the six-yard box.

I think Millwall have done well. They have limited Newcastle to half chances and the odd set piece threat. They have made things really difficult for the visitors, crowding them out of space on the edge of the area.

When the home side have advanced up the pitch the Newcastle defence has not looked particularly secure.

As we reach the half-hour mark, Newcastle have 10 shots to Millwall’s one, though they sit one apiece on shots on target.

Esse gets caught on his heels as Hall pulls a long ball back on the left, and in the crowd at the top of the box Willock takes a shot, pulling it wide – cheers from the home crowd again.

First piece of good attacking play from Millwall as Neghli and Baggott work on the overlap. Baggott lofts a high ball to the back post, where Dykes gets a foot on it on the volley, but he can’t quite get over it and it’s easily picked up by Hornicek.

Barnes and Ramsey combine again down the left, with the midfielder trying to feed Barnes on his run. The pass has too much on it though, and as it runs out the back it’s met with jeers from the home fans for a goal kick.

Wissa breaks away down the centre of the field, with Barnes on his left, using him as a decoy. Wissa takes the shot though and it is blocked by a sliding defender.

Newcastle hit 20 minutes in with 68 per cent possession but nothing to show yet for their efforts. You feel like it will only be a matter of time though.

Another Newcastle corner, swung in well and Botman comes charging in, beating cooper to a free header. The defender heads it over the bar and holds his head in his hands. The visitors could definitely be a goal up by now.

Hall’s free-kick is met by the first man Metcalfe who heads it away to atone for his foul and Newcastle remain stymied.

Millwall will have expected Newcastle to dominate the ball but they are really pushing for an opener, especially down the left side with Barnes and Hall.

Again, Newcastle coming down the wings, this time on the left. Esse picks the ball up but loses it and Willock picks it up and takes a shot on his right foot with good power but sends it straight at Marschall. The debut keeper parries it away and it’s cleared by a  Millwall header.

Willock comes down the left soon after and is fouled by Metcalfe to get a free kick in a good spot outside the box.

Murphy gets a shot off after Dedic picks up a long ball on the right side and crosses it back towards the middle of the field. Murphy gets on it and takes the shot inside the box off his left foot but it sails over the bar.

González gives the ball away cheaply and Metcalfe picks it up, but unable to move it forward.

Newcastle will need to make sure they don’t get complacent in defence.

Millwall having a spell of possession, the counter-attack looking like their best option but as they move down the right hand side, Lovelace makes a late challenge to get the ball back and fouls Wissa.

Newcastle advancing, with Dedic and Ramsey moving the ball across midfield. Barnes gets the ball on the left of the box, and his ball is in knocked out and Newcastle get the first corner of the game.

Nothing comes of it as it is sent in high and long over the box.

Fair to say both teams are settling, but Millwall try and create a chance with Lovelace, though it’s intercepted. Dykes takes a bit of a knock and is slow to get up.

Here we go in south London, and Millwall get us started.

Just a reminder of the teams starting today:

Starting XI: Filip Marschall; Jordi Osei-Tutu, Caleb Taylor, Jake Cooper, Elkan Baggott; Lyndon Dykes, Jenson Metcalfe; Camiel Neghli, Daniel Kelly, Romain Esse; Zak Lovelace

Substitutes: Regan Monty, Tristan Parkes, Sacha Vieira, George Beaumont, Yanis Issoufou, George Evans, Taïryk Arconte, Alfie Massey, Zak Sturge

Starting XI: Lukás Hornícek; Lewis Hall, Fabian Schär, Amar Dedic, Sven Botman; Jacob Murphy, Nico González; Jacob Ramsey, Harvey Barnes, Joe Willock; Yoane Wissa

Substitutes: Tino Livramento, Anthony Elanga, Malick Thiaw, Nick Pope, Lewis Miley, Bazoumana Touré, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Aladji Bamba, Sean Steur

The teams are coming out of the tunnel, and both home and away fans in the Den are already in loud voice. Kick off on the way!

"We've tried to find the right balance" ⚖️Matthias Jaissle on his team selection for tonight's match with Millwall ⚫️ pic.twitter.com/kiRRxAgLk8

We’re just a few minutes away from kick off in south London, but Bournemouth have scored the first goal of the third round, with Ryan Christie putting his side ahead against Lincoln.

Alex Neil has not minced his words over his squad’s injury crisis. His team is down 13 players, which the coach says has “definitely forced” his hand in terms of squad rotation.

Playing two matches a week in the “relentless” Championship has turned his squad selection into a “needs must scenario” and he even admitted he “may need to make a couple of changes at half-time depending on how the game goes”

Matthias Jaissle is clearly taking this competition seriously and having started the league well, he is still trying to get the fans onside and create momentum for his team.

At the same time, Telegraph Sport have reported that Ross Wilson, the sporting director, has warned there will have to be more departures in future windows. Having lost Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães in 12 months, there will be yet be more upheaval.

You can read Luke Edwards’ full story on that here

The Premier League teams playing in European competitions enter the EFL Cup in this round, with all 16 fixtures being played over five match days. As well as tonight’s games there will be:

Fleetwood Town vs Sheffield United (7.45pm)

*all kick-off at 8pm, unless stated otherwise

Newcastle have named a strong side – probably the strongest they could field when factoring in senior players needing game time – to take on Millwall in the Carabao Cup.

Jacob Ramsey impressed coming off the bench against Bournemouth last weekend and manager Matthias Jaissle refused to sanction winger Jacob Murphy’s transfer to Nottingham Forest late in the window. Both deserve a chance to impress from the start.

Veteran centre back Fabian Schar comes in for Malick Thiaw, but those are the only three changes from the side that drew with Bournemouth.

Jaissle insisted he would take the competition seriously and the teamsheet proves it, but it also raises questions about some of Newcastle’s summer recruitment.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m but was withdrawn at half time in the win over West Brom in the previous round, which means Harvey Barnes does not get a rest. That’s a lot of money to spend on a winger who has not looked Premier League ready so far.

Aladji Bamba, a £30m signing from Monaco, has not started a game yet and has been an unused substitute since the opening game against Liverpool. He remains on the bench.

Even Sean Steur, who has looked good since his summer move from Ajax, cannot dislodge another more recent arrival in former Manchester City midfielder Nico González.

Having made a total of eight new signings in a much-vaunted summer rebuild, Jaissle only started three of them against Bournemouth and only two start tonight at The Den.

Early days but this was one of the main reasons Eddie Howe quit – he did not think the likes of Toure, Steur and Bamba were ready to play first team football.

The visitors have arrived in south London

We've made it to South East London 👋 pic.twitter.com/nh8Fpa37xT

We’re bringing you the action from the pick of tonight’s EFL Cup games but there are also four games kicking off at 7.45pm:

Aston Villa are currently 3-1 up against Club Brugge in Belgium – follow the action here

Manchester City will face Porto at 8.00pm – our live blog has just gone live here with the team news from both sides

Yoane Wissa takes the captain’s armband tonight, while Jacob Ramsey starts up front after scoring a late equaliser against Bournemouth on Saturday

Your Mags at Millwall ✊ pic.twitter.com/zfnHgTlWgh

Keeper Filip Marschall is making his debut while Jensen Metcalfe is back in the squad after his red card against Bolton was overturned on appeal

How your Lions line-up tonight 🔢 pic.twitter.com/wEp6qLIz4Y

Welcome to tonight’s live coverage of Millwall vs Newcastle United, as the Geordies travel to south London for the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Newcastle held off West Brom in their second-round match, with Harvey Barnes scoring two second-half goals to see his side through. It was a mighty comeback, after Isaac Price scored early to stun the crowd at St James’ Park. Bazoumana Toure equalised for Matthias Jaissle’s side just before half-time, and Barnes, his replacement in the second half, put them ahead minutes after the restart. West Brom pulled it back to 2-2 with a penalty converted by Price after Lewis Hall was deemed to have handled the ball in the box, but Barnes got his second just nine minutes from full-time and the hosts were able to see out the match to progress.

Alex Neil’s Millwall have reached round three via a 0-1 win over Cambridge United, following a penalty shoot-out in the first round to beat QPR. They come into this tie with a squad stretched thin, as they have been hit with an injury crisis a month into the new season. Millwall have confirmed that they will be without Casper De Norre, Josh Coburn, Tristan Crama, Alfie Doughty, Mathis Servais, Ryan Leonard, Mihailo Ivanovic, Lukas Jensen and Luke Cundle.

Both sides sit seventh in their respective leagues, with Millwall on a record of three wins and two losses this season, while Newcastle remain unbeaten (two draws and a win).

Newcastle will hoping to progress smoothly in a tournament that they have recently enjoyed good form in – winners in 2025 and semi-finalists last season – and with Millwall dealing with a bare bones squad, the Championship side are the underdogs on paper going into this fixture.

But, as always, anything can happen, so let us know your score prediction in the comments and we’ll be bringing you team news soon!

#1989. Borussia Dortmund vs Elversberg - prediction, team news, lineups

By Lewis Nolan | 05 Nov 2026 21:01

Borussia Dortmund must maintain the pace at the top of the Bundesliga on Saturday, when they welcome Elversberg to Signal Iduna Park.

Black and Yellow are second in the table with 18 points and currently trail Bayern Munich due to goal difference, while newly-promoted Elversberg are in seventh place with 13 points.

Dortmund deserve credit for coming away from Allianz Arena on October 31 with a point, drawing 2-2 with Bayern in their most difficult league game of the season thanks to Fabio Silva's 89th-minute equaliser.

Boss Niko Kovac should be delighted with the result, but it would be understandable if he was frustrated by the fact his side have now drawn three of their last four Bundesliga outings.

A ninth second-placed finish in 15 seasons would be disappointing, though BVB supporters should still be looking forward positively given their team boast the best defensive record in the division this term having conceded just six goals.

The hosts' defensive resilience was on display against Real Betis in the Champions League on Wednesday, when they won 2-1 thanks to second-half strikes form Silva and Konstantinos Karetsas.

That victory was Dortmund's sixth win at Signal Iduna Park in their last seven fixtures at the stadium, a period in which they avoided defeat.

Elversberg returned to winning ways on October 30, beating Mainz 05 4-1, a game in which they led 3-0 at half time and managed to score a fourth before conceding in the 92nd minute.

The success that the visitors have experienced in the Bundesliga should not be underestimated, especially as 30 points were enough to guarantee survival in the top flight in 2025-26, and the club are on track to accumulate 55 points.

Manager Vincent Wagner may have overseen two wins in his team's past three league clashes, but he will still be concerned that his side have lost lost four and drawn one of their last seven matches in all competitions.

Schwarz und Weiss will hope to avoid suffering a third consecutive loss on the road, with the visitors having won only one of their four away Bundesliga contests.

Elversberg netted eight goals in those four away games, while all four of the goals they have scored on the road in the league came in a 4-3 victory against Borussia Monchengladbach in matchweek one.

Borussia Dortmund form (all competitions):

Dortmund's injury list is starting to clear up, with only Emre Can (knee), Justin Lerma (muscle) and Giannis Konstantelias (knee) confirmed to be on the sidelines, while the first two are set to return this month.

Kovac is likely to field a three-man defence consisting of Joane Gadou, Waldemar Anton and Nico Schlotterbeck, stationing the trio behind Jobe Bellingham and Felix Nmecha.

Striker Serhou Guirassy is a slight doubt, but even if he is available, it may be better to avoid any risks with his fitness by starting Silva up front.

As for Elversberg, the absence of defenders Jan Gyamerah (hamstring) and Luis Seifert (ankle) could lead to the selection of Luca Sirch, Lukas Pinckert, Maximilian Rohr and Lesse Gunther in the backline.

Centre-forward David Mokwa registered an assist against Mainz, though he will be keen to find the back of the net himself on Saturday.

Borussia Dortmund possible starting lineup:

Kobel; Gadou, Anton, Schlotterbeck; Ryerson, Bellingham, Nmecha, Svensson; Beier, Chukwuemeka; Silva

Kristof; Sirch, Pinckert, Rohr, Gunther; Keidel, Poreba; Petkov, Onyeka, Krattenmacher; Mokwa

Elversberg will almost certainly prove to be challenging opponents given their impressive display last time out.

However, their record away from home is far from perfect, while BVB have been excellent at home, so perhaps Dortmund will be able to keep the pressure on Bayern.
